title: "Papa Jack" Laine and Alfred Laine Interview, 1951-04-21

blocks.x: For the 21st, and I'm down at Papa Jack Lane's house at 521 Clouette Street. Mrs. Lane is right alongside of us both, chaperoning this party. And I wanted to ask Jack a few questions, if you'd be kind enough to answer. Jack, what is your full name?

My full name is George Lane. George V Lane. I was born here in the state, never was out of the state in my life. The farthest I've been was New York or Chicago or something of that sort, but never out of the state. And I've been playing music since I was a boy, I reckon about eight years old. And of course... Wait a minute, you didn't tell us the date of your birth, Jack. Well, I was born in 1873 on the 21st day of September. And ever since then, why, I enjoyed music the best of anyone should like it as much as I did.
Well, you started telling me that you were about eight years old when you started to play music. What instrument did you fool with then?

When I first started, I started playing drums. And how I come to play this drum, it was during the time of the exposition. It was up at around the Audubon Park. Well, Jack, you know I have a faint recollection that somewhere around December of 1884,

the Cotton Exposition was held in Audubon Park. But this is purely a guess on my part. And after the exposition was over, there was a couple old instruments laying around there, and my dad brought me home an old drum.

And from that time on, I've been playing music up until the first war. Jack, what other instruments besides drum did you play? Well, I played a little alto, but I wouldn't crow so much about that, because it was very little that I played of it.
But I played quite a number of times in the band with it, and made out good. And outside of that, I played a little bass fiddle also.

Then I kept on my drums right on. I played... What were the drums called? A bass drum and a kettle drum? Was that what they were called in the early days? Yes, they were. I was a bass drum. I was a bass drum. I was a bass drum.
I was a bass drum. I was a bass drum. Yes, they were called trap drums in the early days.
And of course, we had a lot of better traps mixed up with it, like bells and tom-toms and stuff of that sort. But we had to use them also in different pieces, in different numbers.
How old were you when you bought your own first set of drums?
Well, I must have been around about 12, 14 years old when I got my first set of drums.
And how old were you when you had your own first band?

Well, I was doing... when I had my own band, I was doing the Spanish and American War. I had then, in the Spanish and American War, I had 35 pieces, including myself. And after that, well before that rather, I used to play music right on, play field band music in different kinds of instruments with different kinds of musicians. that is different members of different organizations that came with me. And the line of a lot of children that I used to have. Very lot of children. And brought them all in. And ever since then, why, they began picking up playing music. And they made remarkable good musicians out there. Jack, was your daddy a musician? No, my father never knew anything at all about any interest.
Well, who is the gentleman that taught you how?

Well, the man that I first started with was Dave Perkins. And ever since Dave Perkins, I went with another guy that used to play. His name was Meade, Will Meade. He was an awful good professor. Well, now that's been some years ago. He had a cigar stand on Royal and Espenade. That's where I used to go to. He was a mighty nice musician too.
Jack, how far from this section that we are right now have you lived? Have you always lived in this neck of the woods? Well, Doctor, fortunately I did.

Right in this neighborhood all my life. From, say, Mandeville Street, which is only four squares from here, down to this hill, Clot Street. Uh-huh. In all my days I lived just in that same, in this same territory.
Uh, Jack, now another interest that you've had too, you've been a member of the Volunteer Fires Association, haven't you? That's right. Well, how many years you been in that?

Well, fortunately that I made one, one or two parades with them when they, uh, consolidated into, uh, a pay department. I see. Liquidated and went into a pay department. I see. But since then, I joined another company, which is Davy Crockett. They're over the river. I'm in there now around about, well, about 45 years, something long in there. Any, any other men still in that been in that long? Well, yes. I, just recently, the day before yesterday, when the dedication of the Tulane Avenue, uh, Lane, was open, I met one of the oldest men was in that, uh, company. And that company is now 110 year old. I see.
Jack, uh, can you remember the names of the first men that were, played music with you in your first professional band? Can you recall their names? Well, quite a number of them, I can, yes.

When I first organized, uh, uh, playing string music, and, uh, into a brass band, returned into a brass band, I had a man by the name of Bakke, uh, Shail Bakke, uh, Bega, Lawrence Bega, uh, had, uh, uh, uh, Bill Gallaty, Willie Guitarr. Now, there's a coincidence for you. This man, Willie Guitarr, that was his real name, Willie Guitarr. He played bass fiddle, and he lived on Music Street. Well, he's a mighty, mighty good bass player. Page and Mr. Ripley, huh? Exactly, exactly. Then I had... Jack, would you continue telling us, uh, the rest of the men that you played, not necessarily the very first band,
but approximately the very early bands,
what other names could come to your mind? Well, I'm not sure what you played, but what other names could come to your mind?
Well, I'm not sure what you played, but what you played, what you played, what you played, what you played, what you played, what you played, what you played, what you played, what you played.

Well, uh, in the first bands that I've organized, Manuel Malo, uh, Leon Malo, uh, had, uh, Frank Christian, uh, Emil Christian, and, uh, uh, uh, I can't think of his other name now. Uh, Charlie Christian. That's right. Charlie Christian. Charlie Christian. And, uh, uh, also, I had, uh, a gentleman, a fellow by the name of Ginnerman, he lived on, uh, Jackson Avenue. Well, of course, there's quite a number of these men.
Any lawyer candidates with you?

Yes, I've had the lawyer candidates, both. Son and father playing lots of jobs with me, but the first time when, when I first organized, they played, especially the old man. He was with me. He was one of my members of the first, first band. Now, I had, uh, all together, I used to master seven bands up, up until, uh, the war, the world's war, first world's war. And, of course, a lot of the men, they went with, uh, they were drafted, and went, of course, in the army. Did they all have your name,
Jack Lane's band? No, I had Reliance band,

one band named Reliance, the other name, Tuxedo, and the other name, Lane. Different names like that, you understand? And, of course, split bands, well, they'd go out all together, under the name of Lane, would be the split bands, you see? I wouldn't give them the right name, because they were from the different bands. I see. Members of the different bands. Well, then we'd carry on from there. Jack, what about the, uh, minstrels? Didn't you say? Well,
then we'd carry on from there. Jack, you've got minstrels. Didn't you ever have any minstrels?
I did. I had a minstrel, called, uh, Lane's Great Majestic Minstrels.
How long did they last? Well,

uh, we started out of town with this show, and we got as far as Vitsburg, when they wouldn't let us go no further on the kind of smallpox, and the money panic was on doing. I, I reckon a greater many, many people today remembers that money panic we had here, and the smallpox through the country. That's right. Of course, that stopped me from going any further. It's an,
it's an interesting thing, Jack. My grandfather was president of the Louisiana State Board of Health when that epidemic was going on. Well,

and it was just that time, Doctor. Sure. Well, of course, we had to come back. Well, then I played around town here, whole different lots, all around town, all over in Algiers, and I made pretty good, but still, and all this smallpox epidemic and all that sort of stuff, I just closed down and went out of that business.
Jack, can you remember this? When is the first parade that you marched in? Well,

no, I really couldn't, but I remember though... Approximately. I remember one time, that, it started to snow on the Mardi Gras day. That was the first big Mardi Gras parade ever I made. It started to snow one time, but I don't remember just now, the year that was in. But that's been, oh, good gracious, some time ago.

Gee, Jack, I don't see how you can possibly remember all those things when I'm springing on you, this way. It just so happens that I accidentally know that the only snow that was on the road was in the year 1899. And you said just about the turn of the century, you're awfully close there. Did you ever, uh, play more than one job on Mardi Gras day? Yes, indeed I did. I played as high as five jobs, six jobs if you want. I played one Mardi Gras day,

so much music, that the men after they played the ball for the Merry Whitties Social Club, that they wouldn't come the next day to collect their money. They had to pay for money. They had to pay for money. They had to pay for money. They had to pay for money. They had to pay for money. They had to pay for money. They had to pay for money. They had to pay for money. They had to pay for money. They had to pay for money.
To recuperate.

Exactly, exactly. Now I can, I can, uh, remember some of the jobs I paid that day. The first job I paid that day, it was from seven to half past eight. I think it was for the, uh, Dr. Cabdors, they had some sort of a pill or something, and, uh, they advertised it, like,
uh, an antiseptic.
Like a hadicol, huh? Yeah, something like an antiseptic, you feel. And, uh, from there, from there, we jumped in a wagon and played, uh, an hour and a half, again, for the Merry Whitties Ball.
Now this happened all on one day. Marty Cosa. Jack, was that before the turn of the century, or after?

After. Uh, then I played, uh, the advertisement of the Merry Whitties Ball. And from there, we jumped up to, uh, St. Charles and Calliope and played the Day Parade. And from the Day Parade, we came all the way down to Frenchman Street, and we played the View of Damascus on Frenchman and Decatur. And from the Frenchman and Decatur, we jumped again in the, in the, uh, wagon, and finished our job playing the advertising for the Merry Whitties Ball. And from then, we jumped up again to Calliope and St. Charles, for the Night Parade. After we got done the Night Parade, we went over to the Lusitanus Hall and played the Merry Whitties Ball. We also played one hour overtime at the ball, an extra hour. Jack, how many men usually comprise your marching bands for the parade? Well, uh,
we used to have, uh, from 12 to 14. But sometimes, I'd have about 18,
in, in the band. I see. Now, what were your little groups that comprised the dance? Well, uh, we used to have,
uh, from 12 to 14. the drums that comprised the dance bands. How many were they?

It all depend on, uh, the, all depend on what, the, the people wanted. If they wanted six men, well, I'd point at them six men. In them days, we used to call it six men, seven pieces, because the trap drums was in there. See? I see. Uh, did the violin ever play with you, Jack? Yes,

indeed. Up to when? Well, oh, we used to have a band. Some would want four. Some would want eight. Some would want ten. Well, what would you consider a, a, uh, jazz band? Just exactly the number of pieces.
Six or seven? Seven. Uh-huh. Seven.
It was,
mostly used.
It was, huh? Mostly used. I see.
Uh,
did the violin ever play with you, Jack?
Yes, indeed. Up to when? Well, oh, to, well, long before the war, then I began to, uh, keep nothing else but, uh, blowing instruments, unless it was necessarily to have, uh,

such a string instrument as a violin. I see. Uh, Jack, one thing more I wanted to ask you. Uh, we read a great deal in the history of jazz and Freddie Kepper. Did you know him? I did. Uh, what about Buddy Bolden? Did you ever know him?
Well, I, I heard of Buddy Bolden, but, uh, I never knew him. But, uh, there was a man by the name of Lopez. He, uh, he was one,
I believe,
one of the Polish colored bands, I think, was in the city. That's right. And, uh, it was during my time.
At that time, he was playing music, and I was playing music at the same time.
I see. Uh, Mrs. Lane, would you say one or two words for us first? Isn't,
isn't your wife's brother? No, cousin.
I see. Uh, Mrs. Lane, would you say one or two words for us first? Isn't, isn't your wife's brother? No, cousin. Uh, uh, uh, uh, uh,

uh, uh, most of the men down here affectionately call you Mama Lane? Yes, uh, Yes, and, uh, uh, isn't it also true that you had a finger in the pie for the firemen around here? I made every shirt they wore. How many sometimes?
I made 42 shirts when they started.
And they were dark, weren't they? What color? Uh-huh. You're in the pot for the farmers around here?
Yes, I made every shirt they wore.
How many sometimes?
I made 42 shirts when they started.
And they were dark, weren't they? What color?
Dark reds. Dark reds.
What color helmets?
They have white and black helmets. I see. And I made the ties and I made grand marshals, regalias and all.
Do you like music?
Yes, I do. I love music.
Well, is there anything you want to say before we sign off?
Well...
Just so that you hope things keep going alright. I hope so, yeah. Okay. Alright, Jack. Jack.
to say a few more words in closing.

Speaking about the fire company, I organized a Dennechine fire company about 15 years ago. And through the help and the assistance of my good wife, we made it a success. It's still progressing today, and we're doing remarkably well. Now, as I said before, we were on that parade up there on Tulane Avenue Wednesday, and made quite a number of people look up at the old days. They remember those days, quite a number of them were on the street, and they remember those days when the old-time volunteers used to parade on a Fort of March. Well, of course, I'm still proud of that, too. And as far as everything that I've went through, I kind of made a success of, which I was thankful to God for the help of it.

I have one or two more words. Jack, many records that the collectors are saving now have been made by two bands, one called the Original Dixieland Jazz Band, and the other one, the New Orleans Rhythm Kings. It's my impression that these were both makeshift bands whose name was coined for the record date. Is that so, or did they exist beforehand? No, that was after the record date. They didn't play together as groups before then? No. Did you ever get different ones and put them together for a date like that?
I sure did, lots of them.
I see. Now, another thing, too. Do you remember Tom Brown and Harry Shields when they used to play in the old days?
Yes, I do remember. I picked them boys up playing with me when they were just small children.
Does the music we play today sound anything like what you used to play?

Well, I dare to say there ain't very much change in it. I think the music you're playing today that you hear now amongst the bands, so-called jazz bands, which they call it jazz today. In my time, it was ragtime. Now, there isn't... You hardly can tell the difference. You hardly can. You've got to take good notice the way the tunes are coming out, them instruments, to detect the difference of those days up until today.

If you'll read anything about the history of ragtime and jazz, a recent authority made the remark that ragtime suddenly died in 1917, it's my contention that no such a thing that had just gradually changed over into something that sounded just a little bit smoother. Is that the difference, really?
That's correct. That's correct.
Well, Jack, I certainly thank you for the interview, and it's been a pleasure, and I hope you go on living and enjoying life as good health as you are now.
I also pray that the boys keeps up the good work.
Okay. Okay.

This is Alfred John Lane. I'm talking about 531 Cluett Street for my daddy right now, and he and I was just now talking, and we were talking about things gone by years ago. Of course, I'm 56 years old today. I'm not a young man, and I was with Jimmy Durante when I was 19 years old. I was in New York playing with Jimmy Durante. I don't think I have much more to say to you, but nevertheless...
Well, didn't you have your own band while your daddy's was called?
Oh, yeah, and I had my band, Baby Lane. My daddy got a band for me, and he started me out playing, so I played with my dad. What instruments did you play? I played a trumpet.
Any other instruments? Well, yeah. I, yeah, yeah. I, yeah, yeah. I, yeah, yeah.
